stem: Which of the following brainstem nuclei is NOT located in the pons:
fact: The pons houses nuclei of the trigeminal, abducens, facial, and vestibulocochlear nerves. The trochlear nucleus lies in the midbrain.
mnemonic: Trochlear travels through the midbrain; V, VI, VII, and VIII are pontine neighbours.
finding: The original page displays trochlear nucleus as correct; NCBI places cranial nerve IV with the midbrain and describes the pons as containing the relevant V–VIII nuclei.

stem: A 25 year old woman presents to ED complaining of unsteadiness of her feet and slurred speech. On examination she demonstrates past-pointing, she is unable to perform the heel-shin test and she has nystagmus. The lesion would most likely be in the:
fact: The combination of past-pointing, impaired heel-shin testing, gait unsteadiness, slurred speech, and nystagmus localises to the cerebellum. The source lists DANISH signs: dysmetria/dysdiadochokinesia, ataxia, nystagmus, intention tremor, slow/slurred/scanning speech, and hypotonia.
mnemonic: DANISH signs point to the cerebellum.
finding: The original page displays cerebellum as correct and gives the DANISH signs; the PMC review supports cerebellar motor, gait, eye-movement, and speech dysfunction.

stem: What of the following type of visual field defect are you most likely to see in a lesion of the optic radiation in the right parietal lobe:
fact: A right parietal optic-radiation lesion affects superior fibres carrying the contralateral inferior visual field, producing a left homonymous inferior quadrantanopia.
mnemonic: Parietal radiation carries the lower field; right lesion means left loss.
finding: The original page displays left homonymous inferior quadrantanopia as correct; NCBI states that superior fibres traverse the parietal lobe and represent the inferior visual field.

stem: A 40 year old female presents to ED complaining of complete visual loss in her right eye. On fundoscopy you note a pale retina and a cherry red spot. You suspect an emboli. Which of the following blood vessels is most likely the source of the emboli:
fact: The internal carotid artery is the most likely source. The ophthalmic artery arises from the internal carotid artery and supplies the orbit and eyeball; its central retinal artery is an end artery, so occlusion causes monocular blindness.
finding: The original page displays internal carotid artery as correct; NCBI confirms the ophthalmic artery’s ICA origin and retinal supply.

stem: What type of visual field defect are you most likely to see in a lesion of the parietal optic radiation:
fact: A lesion of the parietal optic radiation results in a contralateral homonymous inferior quadrantanopia because the superior radiation fibres represent the inferior visual field.
mnemonic: Parietal = lower quadrant; temporal = upper quadrant.
finding: The original page displays contralateral homonymous inferior quadrantanopia as correct; NCBI corroborates the parietal-radiation mapping.

stem: Transection of the anterolateral tract of the spinal cord results in which of the following clinical features:
options: Loss of pain and temperature sensation
Loss of vibration and fine-touch sensation
fact: Transection of the anterolateral tract results in contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation, beginning approximately one segment below the lesion.
finding: The original page displays loss of pain and temperature sensation as correct and states the contralateral one-segment-below pattern; NCBI identifies the spinothalamic tract as the pain-temperature pathway.

stem: A 65 year old lady presents to ED complaining of sudden onset visual loss. On examination you demonstrate visual loss on the right side of the vertical midline with macular sparing in both eyes. Which of the following blood vessels is most likely occluded:
fact: The posterior cerebral artery supplies the occipital visual cortex. An occipital lesion causes a contralateral homonymous hemianopia, often with macular sparing.
mnemonic: PCA perfuses the visual cortex in the occipital lobe.
finding: The original page displays posterior cerebral artery as correct and describes macular-sparing homonymous loss; NCBI identifies PCA as the main supply to primary visual cortex.

stem: A 65 year old lady, with a history of hypertension and diabetes mellitus, presents to ED with a 1 hour history of sudden onset of weakness and numbness solely in her left leg and foot. She is placed on the stroke pathway. Which of the following blood vessels has most likely been occluded:
fact: The anterior cerebral artery supplies the medial cerebral hemisphere, including the paracentral lobule representing motor and sensory function of the lower limb.
mnemonic: ACA = Anterior Cerebral Artery for the Ankle and leg.
finding: The original page displays anterior cerebral artery as correct and explains medial-hemisphere/paracentral-lobule lower-limb localisation.

stem: You are performing a full neurological examination on a patient who has presented to the ED department with generalised weakness. You note she has a unilateral absence of her triceps reflex. Which spinal nerve is primarily responsible for this reflex:
fact: The triceps tendon reflex predominantly tests spinal cord segment C7 and is mediated through the radial nerve.
mnemonic: C7 extends the elbow: triceps reflex.
finding: The original page displays C7 as correct; NCBI identifies the triceps reflex as predominantly C7.

stem: The primary visual cortex is located in which of the following regions:
fact: The primary visual cortex is located in the occipital lobe along the calcarine fissure and is responsible for initial cortical visual processing.
finding: The original page displays occipital lobe as correct; NCBI locates V1 along the calcarine fissure in the occipital lobe.
